newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Economists wary of German trade J-curve.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Economists wary of German trade J-curve.

text.p: Germany's trade surplus widened in 1996 from the year before, showing that exports remain the strength of the economy, but analysts warned the J-curve effect of the strong dollar could begin to threaten that improvement.

A weak mark should help boost German exports over the long term, but economists fear that in the initial months the so called J-curve effect may depress the trade surplus by boosting the mark value of dollar-denominated imports.
As high unemployment and consumer uncertainty damp domestic demand, the strength of the export sector underscores the feeble state of the rest of Germany's upswing, they said.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, hard pressed to get a grip on Bonn's deficit to qualify for the planned single European currency, is trying to cut social spending without throttling government investment.
A weakening in the export sector could pull the rug out from under those efforts, the economists said.

The Federal Statistics Office said on Tuesday the 1996 trade surplus rose to 97.6 billion marks from 85.3 billion in 1995. Exports rose 4.6 percent to 784.3 billion marks while imports rose 3.4 percent to 686.7 billion marks.
In December alone the trade surplus was 7.2 billion marks, down from 9.8 billion marks in November but up from 6.4 billion marks in December 1995.
"The data still show export-led growth. The current-account deficit also declined, which is very fortunate," said economist Holger Schmieding at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
"But the pace of improvement could slow significantly in the next few months because of the weak mark."
The current account, which includes services as well as visible trade, showed a deficit of 26.6 billion marks in 1996, narrowing from 29.9 billion marks the previous year.
The dollar has been on a rocket since the start of the year, climbing above 1.70 marks on Tuesday to set new 34-month highs, up from about 1.47 marks a year ago.

Economic growth data for the fourth quarter, due for issue on Wednesday, are expected to show a diminished contribution by net exports and a slight contraction of about 0.2 percent in economic output from the previous quarter.
Eckhard Schulte, economist at Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt, said the J-curve effect could present a near-term obstacle, but its impact should fade in the second half of 1997.

"We still expect exports to account for about half of economic growth this year," Schulte said. He sees 1997 growth in German GDP at about 2.0 percent this year, less than the government's projection of 2.5 percent growth.
"The outlook still isn't good for domestic demand," he said.
